title: HTTP Status Code Selection
description: Select the correct HTTP status codes for every API operation, including 2xx success, 3xx redirects, 4xx client errors, and 5xx server errors.

data.text: HTTP status codes are the primary error communication mechanism in REST APIs. Using the wrong code confuses clients, breaks retry logic, and makes debugging harder. This lesson maps every common API operation to the correct status code.

rows: No token, expired token, bad signature
Valid JSON but invalid business data

data.title: Consistent error response structure across all 4xx and 5xx codes
data.content: Use a consistent JSON structure so clients can parse errors without special-casing each code.

data.title: Anti-patterns to avoid
items: Returning 200 OK with an error field in the body — this breaks HTTP semantics
Returning 500 for validation errors — clients cannot programmatically distinguish validation from server failure
Returning 404 for authorization failures — this leaks information about which IDs exist
Returning different error structures per endpoint — clients need a unified parser

data.title: 404 vs 403 for auth
data.text: Return 404 (not 403) for resources the user does not have permission to see. This prevents attackers from enumerating valid IDs by observing whether a resource exists.

data.title: Different outcomes for the same endpoint
data.content: A well-designed endpoint returns the correct status code for every possible outcome.

items.question: Should I ever return 200 for a failed operation?
items.answer: No. A 200 OK signals success. If the operation failed, return the appropriate 4xx or 5xx code. Clients use status codes for control flow; mixing success and failure in 200 breaks retry and logging logic.

items.question: When should I use 422 vs 400?
items.answer: Use 400 for syntactic errors (malformed JSON, missing required headers). Use 422 for semantic errors (valid JSON but invalid business data, failed validation rules).

items.question: Is it okay to return 500 with a stack trace?
items.answer: Never in production. Stack traces leak internal architecture details that attackers can exploit. Return a generic error message and log the full trace server-side with the request ID.

data.title: Key takeaway
points: Status codes are part of the API contract; choose them deliberately.
Use 200 for success, 4xx for client errors, 5xx for server errors.
Use a consistent error body structure across all error codes.
data.takeaway: HTTP status codes are the most reliable error signal in a distributed system. Get them right and your clients can write correct retry, fallback, and debugging logic automatically.
